content: The systematic reviews were conducted to update the World Health Organization (WHO) Guideline on country pharmaceutical pricing policies. The primary authors of this work include David Tordrup, Rianne van den Ham, Christine Leopold, Iris Joosse, Julie Glanville, Eleanor Kotas, and Aukje Mantel-Teeuwisse. The authors are affiliated with the Utrecht Centre for Pharmaceutical Policy and Regulation at Utrecht University in the Netherlands and the York Health Economics Consortium in the United Kingdom. The WHO Guideline on country pharmaceutical pricing policies, second edition, was published in 2020. This guideline provides evidence-based recommendations to assist countries in implementing effective pharmaceutical pricing policies. The systematic reviews were commissioned to ensure that the recommendations reflect the most current evidence and to address additional policy questions related to pharmaceutical pricing. The publication is available under a Creative Commons license, allowing for non-commercial use, redistribution, and adaptation, provided the work is appropriately cited. However, the use of the WHO logo is not permitted, and any adaptations must be licensed under the same or an equivalent Creative Commons license. If a translation of the work is created, a disclaimer must be included, stating that the translation was not created by WHO and that WHO is not responsible for its content or accuracy. The systematic reviews aimed to evaluate the effects of ten pharmaceutical pricing policies on outcomes such as price, volume, availability, and affordability of pharmaceutical products. These policies were assessed individually or in combination, with consideration of contextual factors and implementation strategies that might influence their effectiveness. The specific objectives included estimating the effect size of pricing policies, developing GRADE evidence profiles to assess the strength and quality of evidence, and describing practical and contextual considerations for policy implementation. The report is structured into 13 sections, beginning with a background section. Subsequent sections detail the search methodology, results of the literature search, and conclusions for each of the ten policy topics. These topics include pooled procurement, value-based pricing, discounts for single-source pharmaceuticals, cost-plus pricing, tax exemptions or reductions for pharmaceuticals, interventions promoting the use of quality-assured generic and biosimilar medicines, reference pricing, interventions promoting price transparency, mark-up regulation across the pharmaceutical supply chain, and tendering and negotiation. A common bibliography and detailed appendices on search strategies and excluded studies are also included. The systematic reviews were conducted following the principles outlined in the Cochrane Handbook and guidance from the Centre for Reviews and Dissemination. The reviews addressed two overarching research questions: (1) Which pharmaceutical pricing policies are effective in managing the prices of pharmaceutical products, considering their impacts on volume, availability, and affordability? (2) What contextual factors and implementation strategies may influence the effects of a specific pricing policy? The scope of the review included studies comparing eligible interventions against other interventions, options, or counterfactuals, including historical comparisons. Single policies or combinations of policies were eligible for inclusion, provided they described a comparator or counterfactual. Key pricing policies reviewed include: 1. External Reference Pricing (ERP): This involves using the price of a pharmaceutical product in one or more countries to derive a benchmark or reference price for setting or negotiating the price in a given country. 2. Internal Reference Pricing: This refers to using the prices of identical or similar medicines within a country to derive a reference price for setting or negotiating the price or reimbursement of a product. 3. Value-Based Pricing: Prices for new medicines are set based on their therapeutic value, often assessed through health technology assessment (HTA). 4. Cost-Plus Pricing: This policy considers production costs, promotional expenses, research and development, administrative costs, overheads, and profit to determine a price. 5. Mark-Up Regulation: This involves setting price thresholds, such as maximum prices or mark-up percentages, to regulate wholesale and retail mark-ups in the pharmaceutical supply chain. 6. Promoting Price Transparency: This entails sharing and disclosing information related to medicine prices to ensure accountability. 7. Price Discounts for Single-Source Pharmaceuticals: Discounts are price reductions granted to specific purchasers under certain conditions, such as managed-entry agreements or risk-sharing agreements. 8. Promoting the Use of Quality-Assured Generic and Biosimilar Medicines: Strategies are directed at patients, prescribers, or pharmacists to encourage the use of generic or biosimilar medicines. 9. Tendering and Negotiation: Prices are determined through competitive procurement processes or negotiations among suppliers of identical or comparable medicines. 10. Tax Exemptions or Reductions for Pharmaceuticals: This involves reducing or exempting taxes on medicines to improve affordability. The search strategy for the systematic reviews was developed to address all ten topics and was initially created in MEDLINE syntax before being translated to other databases. The strategy included 12 concepts, such as pharmaceutical pricing policies, reference pricing, value-based pricing, cost-plus pricing, mark-up regulation, price transparency, pooled procurement, and competitive pricing. The systematic reviews provide an updated synthesis of evidence to inform the WHO Guideline on country pharmaceutical pricing policies, ensuring that the recommendations are based on the most current and robust evidence available.
